ca-alcohol-01.question: At what blood-alcohol level does driving become a per se crime (DUI) in California for a driver 21 or older, regardless of visible impairment (CVC § 23152(b))?

options.a: 0.08% (blood alcohol content by weight)
options.c: 0.00% (absolute zero)

ca-alcohol-01.explanation: CVC § 23152(b) makes driving at 0.08% or more blood alcohol (by weight) a crime regardless of driving behavior. 0.08% converts to roughly 0.8 per mille — well above Germany's 0.5-per-mille limit under § 24a StVG. California's subsection (a) separately still allows a DUI charge below 0.08% if actual impairment is proven.

ca-alcohol-02.question: What blood-alcohol threshold applies under CVC § 23152(d) to a person driving a commercial motor vehicle (e.g. a truck or bus requiring a commercial license class) in California?

options.a: 0.08%, the same as for all other drivers

ca-alcohol-02.explanation: For commercial-vehicle drivers, CVC § 23152(d) halves the threshold to 0.04% (about 0.4 per mille) compared with 0.08% for ordinary drivers. Germany applies a comparable extra layer of strictness for drivers who transport passengers or goods professionally, even though the formal 0.5-per-mille limit does not change.

ca-alcohol-03.question: California's 'zero tolerance' law for drivers under 21 (CVC § 23136) bars driving once blood alcohol reaches what level, as measured by a preliminary screening or chemical test?

options.d: 0.00% — an exact zero reading must be shown

ca-alcohol-03.explanation: CVC § 23136(a) sets the under-21 threshold at 0.01% (about 0.1 per mille) — not literally zero, because test instruments have a margin of error, but a de facto zero-tolerance line. Germany regulates novice and under-21 drivers through § 24c StVG with a true 0.0-per-mille limit. A § 23136 violation is a civil license action, not a criminal charge — prosecution under §§ 23152/23153 remains separately possible.

ca-alcohol-04.question: Beyond the zero-tolerance rule, California has a separate offense specifically for drivers under 21 with a blood-alcohol level of 0.05% or more. Which provision is that?
ca-alcohol-04.explanation: CVC § 23140(a) creates a third, middle threshold for drivers under 21 at 0.05% (about 0.5 per mille) — between the 0.01% zero-tolerance line (§ 23136) and the general 0.08% crime (§ 23152). California thus tiers underage drinking-and-driving into three levels, whereas Germany applies a single 0.0-per-mille bar to the same age group.

ca-alcohol-05.question: What does the 'implied consent' rule under CVC § 23612 mean for anyone who drives in California?

options.a: By driving, the person is deemed to have already consented to a chemical alcohol or drug test upon a lawful DUI arrest
options.b: A test may only be administered after a judge issues a prior order
options.c: Taking a test is always voluntary and can be declined without consequence
options.d: The rule applies only to drivers of commercial vehicles

ca-alcohol-05.explanation: CVC § 23612(a) treats consent to chemical testing as already given simply by the act of driving — no separate judicial order is normally needed once a lawful DUI arrest has occurred. In Germany, a blood draw generally requires an order from the prosecutor, a court, or (where delay would risk losing evidence) the police themselves; German law has no blanket 'implied consent' doctrine triggered merely by driving.

ca-alcohol-06.question: A driver is lawfully arrested on suspicion of DUI in California and refuses the chemical test. What consequence does CVC § 23612 attach to that refusal, separate from the outcome of any criminal case?

options.a: None — a test can be declined without any consequence
options.b: A single warning from the officer
options.c: Administrative suspension of the driving privilege by the DMV for at least one year
options.d: Automatic doubling of the fine for the underlying DUI

ca-alcohol-06.explanation: Refusing the test triggers a separate, purely administrative DMV license suspension of at least one year under CVC § 23612, regardless of whether the driver is later convicted of DUI in criminal court. German law has no equally automatic sanction tied solely to refusing a test; the practical consequences there mostly flow later, through how a court weighs the refusal as evidence.

ca-alcohol-07.question: Under CVC § 23612, when the suspicion is alcohol-related DUI, what choice does the driver in California have?

options.a: The driver may substitute a phone call to a lawyer for the chemical test entirely
options.b: The driver may choose between a blood test and a breath test
options.c: The driver may postpone the test to a time of their own choosing
options.d: The driver may have their own personal physician administer the test

ca-alcohol-07.explanation: CVC § 23612 gives the driver a choice between a blood test and a breath test when alcohol is suspected (for drug suspicion, blood is the default, with urine as a fallback). There is expressly no right to consult a lawyer before deciding. This too sets California apart from German procedure, where the method of testing is decided by the ordering authority and the driver has no choice in the matter.

ca-alcohol-08.question: A 16-year-old has held a California 'provisional license' for three months. Under CVC § 12814.6, who is that driver generally barred from carrying as an unsupervised passenger during this period?

options.a: Passengers of any age, without exception
options.b: Passengers under 20 years old, unless a statutory exception applies (e.g. immediate family, medical emergency, commuting to work)
options.c: Only other holders of a provisional license
options.d: No one — the restriction only starts in the second year

ca-alcohol-08.explanation: During the first 12 months after a provisional license is issued, CVC § 12814.6 generally bars carrying passengers under 20 without a parent, guardian, a licensed driver 25 or older, or a certified instructor present; exceptions exist for immediate family and documented emergencies. Germany's comparable model, 'Begleitetes Fahren ab 17' (accompanied driving from 17), instead requires the young driver themselves to have a supervising adult present, with no equivalent age-based cap on who else can ride along.

ca-alcohol-09.question: During what time window is a California provisional license holder generally barred from driving unsupervised in the first 12 months (CVC § 12814.6)?

options.a: 10 p.m. to 6 a.m.
options.b: midnight to 4 a.m.
options.c: 11 p.m. to 5 a.m.
options.d: There is no time restriction, only a passenger restriction

ca-alcohol-09.explanation: CVC § 12814.6 bars unsupervised driving on a provisional license between 11 p.m. and 5 a.m., with the same exceptions (supervision, family, emergency, work/school) as the passenger rule. German law has no fixed nighttime driving curfew for novice drivers of this kind; instead it relies on continuous adult supervision under 'Begleitetes Fahren ab 17'.

ca-alcohol-10.question: A 17-year-old is convicted in California of an alcohol- or drug-related offense under CVC § 13202.5. What outcome does the statute require the court to impose?

options.a: A one-year suspension of the driving privilege, even if the offense had nothing to do with actually driving
options.b: A fine only, with no effect on the driving privilege
options.c: A mere recommendation to the DMV that it consider revoking the license
options.d: Suspension only on a second conviction

ca-alcohol-10.explanation: CVC § 13202.5 requires the court to suspend the driving privilege for one year upon conviction of a person aged 13 to 21 for specified alcohol or drug offenses — even when the underlying act, such as underage possession of alcohol, had nothing to do with actually driving. In Germany, by contrast, license suspension is generally tied to a traffic-related offense or to doubts about fitness to drive (§ 3 StVG together with the fitness-to-drive register), not automatically triggered by any alcohol or drug offense committed by a minor.

ca-speed-01.question: What does the "basic speed law" in CVC § 22350 actually prohibit?

options.a: Any speed above the posted number, regardless of conditions
options.b: Any speed under 25 mph in town
options.c: A speed that is not reasonable or prudent given weather, visibility, traffic, and the surface and width of the highway
options.d: Any speed faster than the slowest vehicle in traffic

ca-speed-01.explanation: CVC § 22350 requires a speed reasonable for the conditions regardless of the posted number — driving the full limit in fog or rain can still violate this law. The closest German rule is § 3(1) StVO (Sichtfahrgebot), which works similarly, but Germany also has fixed numeric limits everywhere except sections of the Autobahn, where only a recommended 130 km/h (Richtgeschwindigkeit) applies.

ca-speed-02.question: Absent special posting (and outside the exception in § 22356), what is the general maximum speed on a California highway under CVC § 22349(a)?

options.a: 55 mph
options.b: 65 mph
options.c: 70 mph
options.d: 75 mph

ca-speed-02.explanation: § 22349(a) sets 65 mph (about 105 km/h) as the general maximum unless a higher limit up to 70 mph has been posted under § 22356. Unlike German Autobahnen, where many stretches carry no speed limit at all, California has essentially no unrestricted road.

ca-speed-03.question: On a two-lane, undivided highway (one through lane each direction), what is the default limit under CVC § 22349(b) unless a higher speed has been posted?

options.a: 55 mph
options.b: 65 mph
options.c: 70 mph
options.d: 45 mph

ca-speed-03.explanation: § 22349(b) lowers the limit on narrow, undivided highways with only one through lane per direction to 55 mph (about 89 km/h) unless the road has been specifically posted for a higher speed. Passing lanes don't count toward the second through lane.

ca-speed-04.question: Absent other posted signs, what prima facie speed limit applies in a business or residence district in California under CVC § 22352?

options.a: 15 mph
options.b: 25 mph
options.c: 35 mph
options.d: 30 mph

ca-speed-04.explanation: § 22352(b)(1) sets 25 mph (about 40 km/h) as the default in business and residence districts without needing a sign — the limit follows from the surrounding development itself. Germany's comparable default urban limit under § 3(3) StVO is a notably higher 50 km/h.

ca-speed-05.question: What prima facie speed limit does CVC § 22352(a)(3) apply to any alley in California?

options.a: 5 mph
options.b: 10 mph
options.c: 20 mph
options.d: 15 mph

ca-speed-05.explanation: § 22352(a)(3) automatically sets 15 mph (about 24 km/h) for any alley, with no sign required. German law has no automatic number for such minor ways — the general urban limit of 50 km/h usually applies unless the area is marked a Verkehrsberuhigter Bereich (walking pace only).

ca-speed-06.question: Under CVC § 22356, after an engineering and traffic survey and proper posting, what is the highest speed Caltrans may set on qualifying freeway segments?

options.a: 75 mph
options.b: 70 mph
options.c: 80 mph
options.d: There is no longer any cap

ca-speed-06.explanation: § 22356 allows Caltrans (with CHP concurrence) to post up to a maximum of 70 mph (about 113 km/h) on qualifying segments — no higher figure is legally available. Anyone driving faster violates the posted limit. California has nothing resembling an unrestricted German Autobahn stretch.

ca-speed-07.question: Under CVC § 22348(b), what happens if someone in California is caught driving over 100 mph?

options.a: Nothing special — 100 mph carries no separate offense as long as the road is clear
options.b: It automatically becomes a felony carrying jail time
options.c: It is a distinct infraction with a fine, and the court may also suspend the person's driving privilege
options.d: A penalty is only imposed starting with the third offense

ca-speed-07.explanation: § 22348(b) makes exceeding 100 mph (about 161 km/h) its own infraction, carrying a fine of up to $500 on a first offense, and the court may also suspend the person's license for up to 30 days; fines and suspensions escalate on repeat offenses. In Germany a comparable speed would also draw a fine, points, and a driving ban depending on location, but German law has no equivalent fixed 100-mph threshold offense.

ca-speed-08.question: Under CVC § 21654(a), where must a vehicle traveling slower than the normal flow of traffic in that direction drive?

options.a: In the right-hand lane, or as close as practicable to the right-hand edge, except when passing or turning left
options.b: In the middle of the roadway so it can be passed from either side
options.c: On the shoulder, as soon as it is below the general limit
options.d: In the left lane, so it will not be overtaken on the right

ca-speed-08.explanation: § 21654(a) requires slower vehicles to use the right-hand lane or the right edge of the roadway, except when passing or preparing to turn left; failing to do so is even treated as prima facie evidence of a violation under subsection (b). This resembles Germany's Rechtsfahrgebot (§ 2 StVO), but in California it applies explicitly to every road, not just to the Autobahn.

ca-speed-09.question: On a two-lane highway (one lane per direction) where passing is unsafe due to oncoming traffic, what must a slow vehicle do under CVC § 21656 once five or more vehicles have queued up behind it?

options.a: Speed up until it reaches the posted limit
options.b: Pull off at the nearest suitable turnout to let the following vehicles pass
options.c: Continue in the opposing lane until a turnout appears
options.d: Stop where it is and activate its hazard lights

ca-speed-09.explanation: § 21656 requires a slow vehicle with five or more vehicles queued behind it to pull off at the nearest designated or suitable turnout to let following traffic pass. German law has no comparably specific trigger of five vehicles; § 4 StVO only requires more generally that drivers avoid obstructing traffic.

ca-speed-10.question: A highway outside a business or residence district has two clearly marked lanes in the same direction. Under CVC § 21754, may a driver overtake on the right there?

options.a: No — passing on the right is prohibited in California under all circumstances
options.b: Only with special permission from the California Highway Patrol
options.c: Yes, because there are enough marked lanes moving in the same direction
options.d: Only at night, when traffic is light

ca-speed-10.explanation: § 21754 permits passing on the right when, outside a business or residence district, there are two or more clearly marked lanes moving in the same direction, as well as when the vehicle ahead is turning left, or on a one-way street. This is a sharp contrast with Germany, where passing on the right outside town is generally prohibited under § 5 StVO (except in slow-moving lane traffic) — a German driver could easily assume, wrongly, that it's always banned in California too.

ca-stops-01.question: At an intersection with no signs or signals at all, two vehicles from different streets arrive at the same time. Who has the right-of-way?

options.a: The vehicle approaching from the right has the right-of-way.
options.b: The vehicle approaching from the left has the right-of-way.
options.c: The larger vehicle has the right-of-way.
options.d: Whichever driver honks first may go first.

ca-stops-01.explanation: CVC § 21800(b)(1) requires that when two vehicles enter an intersection at the same time, the driver on the left yields to the vehicle on their immediate right. This is the same principle as German "rechts vor links" at unsigned intersections - one of the rare cases where California and Germany actually agree.

ca-stops-02.question: At an intersection with no signs, vehicle A has already entered the intersection when vehicle B approaches from another street. B is approaching from A's right. Who must yield?

options.a: Vehicle A, because B is coming from the right.
options.b: Neither - a vehicle from the right always has priority no matter what is already in the intersection.
options.c: Vehicle B, because A has already entered the intersection.
options.d: It depends on which street is the main road.

ca-stops-02.explanation: CVC § 21800(a) gives priority to whichever vehicle has already entered the intersection, over anyone arriving later - the "yield to the right" rule in § 21800(b) only applies when vehicles truly arrive at the same time. Unlike Germany's system of signed priority roads, an unsigned California intersection has no major/minor street distinction at all.

ca-stops-03.question: At an intersection with stop signs on all four approaches (a four-way stop), two vehicles from different streets come to a stop at the same time. Who may proceed first?

options.a: Both may go at once as long as their paths do not cross.
options.b: The vehicle that is to the other driver's right goes first.
options.c: The vehicle on the wider street goes first.
options.d: There is no fixed rule - drivers settle it with hand signals.

ca-stops-03.explanation: CVC § 21800(c) covers the "four-way stop" - a control scheme Germany essentially does not use. When several vehicles stop at the same time, the yield-to-the-right rule applies again, exactly as it does for other unsignaled arrivals under § 21800(b).

ca-stops-04.question: A driver stops at an ordinary stop sign (not one of a four-way stop). Must they wait until the road is completely free of any traffic before proceeding?

options.a: Yes, any visible vehicle blocks them from proceeding.
options.b: No, they only have to yield to vehicles close enough to constitute an immediate hazard.
options.c: Yes, but only if the vehicle is a truck.
options.d: No, they may drive off immediately after stopping regardless of approaching traffic.

ca-stops-04.explanation: CVC § 21802(a) only requires yielding to traffic already in the intersection or close enough to be an immediate hazard - not to every vehicle visible in the distance. Under § 21802(b), once you have yielded, you may proceed, and other approaching traffic must then yield to you.

ca-stops-05.question: At a stop sign, a limit line is painted on the roadway before the crosswalk. Where exactly must the driver stop?

options.a: At the marked limit line.
options.b: Always at the edge of the intersection, regardless of any markings.
options.c: Right on the crosswalk, for a better view of the intersection.
options.d: Anywhere within about 10 meters of the intersection - the law does not specify.

ca-stops-05.explanation: CVC § 22450(a) sets a clear order: stop at the limit line if one is marked; otherwise before the crosswalk; and only if neither exists, at the entrance to the intersecting road. Germany has a very similar concept with its own Haltelinie markings.

ca-stops-06.question: A stop sign is posted at a railroad crossing without gates. What does the law require for stopping there?

options.a: It is enough to slow down noticeably and then continue through.
options.b: A stop is only required if a train is actually visible.
options.c: The driver must stop at the limit line, or, if none is marked, before the first track.
options.d: A stop is only required between 6 a.m. and 10 p.m.

ca-stops-06.explanation: CVC § 22450(b) requires a full stop at the limit line, or before the first track if none is marked, whenever a stop sign is posted at a railroad crossing - regardless of whether a train is currently visible. This is stricter than merely slowing down, which some drivers mistakenly think is enough.

ca-stops-07.question: A driver approaches an intersection controlled by a yield sign (not a stop sign). Must they always come to a complete stop, the way they would at a stop sign?

options.a: Yes, a yield sign always legally requires a complete stop.
options.b: No, they only need to slow or stop as far as necessary to yield to crossing or already-present traffic.
options.c: Yes, but only when pedestrians are standing on the sidewalk.
options.d: No, a yield sign can be completely ignored in California.

ca-stops-07.explanation: CVC § 21803(a) only requires yielding to traffic already in the intersection or on the crossing road - it does not mandate a full stop if it is safe to proceed. This matches the German "Vorfahrt gewähren" sign, which likewise does not require a mandatory stop, unlike the red-and-white stop sign.

ca-stops-08.question: A driver wants to enter a public street from a private driveway or an alley. A vehicle is approaching on the street from the left. Who has the right-of-way?

options.a: The driver entering the street, because the other vehicle is coming from the left.
options.b: Whoever is to the right has priority, just like at a normal intersection.
options.c: Whoever arrived first has the right-of-way.
options.d: The vehicle already on the public street always has the right-of-way; the driver entering must yield.

ca-stops-08.explanation: CVC § 21804(a) requires a driver entering a highway from a driveway, private property, or an alley to yield unconditionally to traffic already on the road - the "yield to the right" rule from § 21800 does not apply here, because this is not two roads of equal standing meeting at an intersection.

ca-stops-09.question: At an intersection, the traffic signal is completely dark due to a power outage (an inoperative signal). What does California law require in this case?

options.a: Every driver must come to a complete stop at the intersection and may then proceed cautiously only when it is safe.
options.b: Whoever would normally have a green light automatically keeps the right-of-way.
options.c: The intersection may not be used at all until the signal is repaired.
options.d: The last signal phase shown before the outage continues to apply.

ca-stops-09.explanation: CVC § 21800(d)(1) requires a complete stop in every direction when a signal is inoperative, with cautious proceeding only afterward; if two vehicles arrive at the same time, yield-to-the-right also applies under § 21800(d)(2). This is stricter than German practice, where a dead traffic light is treated like an unsigned intersection without necessarily requiring a full stop.

ca-stops-10.question: Street A ends right at its intersection with street B, which continues in both directions (a "terminating highway"). Vehicles on A and B reach the unsigned intersection at the same time, and the vehicle on A is approaching from the right. Who has the right-of-way?

options.a: The vehicle on A, because it is approaching from the right.
options.b: Both at once, since there are no signs.
options.c: The vehicle on the continuing street B, regardless of right or left.
options.d: Whichever vehicle is faster.

ca-stops-10.explanation: CVC § 21800(b)(2) defines a "terminating highway" as a street that ends at the intersection instead of continuing through it. Under § 21800(b)(1), a driver on such a terminating street must yield to the continuing street - this overrides the ordinary yield-to-the-right rule. In Germany, a comparable priority would usually be established by a signed priority-road, not automatically by the mere shape of the streets.

ca-turning-01.question: At a signalized intersection in California, the light shows a steady circular red. You want to turn right. Under the California Vehicle Code, what applies if no sign says otherwise?

options.a: You must stop first, then you may turn right on red once you have yielded to pedestrians and to cross traffic that is an immediate hazard.
options.b: Turning right on red is generally prohibited, just like in Germany without a green arrow sign.
options.c: You may turn right without stopping as long as no pedestrian is in the roadway.
options.d: Turning right on red is only allowed at night, not during the day.

ca-turning-01.explanation: CVC § 21453(a) requires stopping at the limit line first. Subdivision (b) then permits turning right on red unless a sign prohibits it, provided pedestrians and cross traffic with an immediate hazard are given the right of way. In Germany, by contrast, turning right on red is only allowed with the special green arrow sign (Grünpfeil) — without it, a red light means a full stop for right-turners too. That is the key contrast German drivers often get wrong.

ca-turning-02.question: You are on a one-way street, stopped at a red light, and the street you want to turn onto is also one-way. What does the California Vehicle Code additionally allow here that would not apply at an ordinary two-way intersection?

options.a: You may proceed straight through the red light if no pedestrian is visible.
options.b: You may turn in any direction on red, including left onto a two-way street.
options.c: After stopping, you may also turn left on red because both streets are one-way, unless a sign prohibits it, while still yielding to pedestrians and cross traffic.
options.d: You may proceed without stopping because one-way streets are exempt from signal control.

ca-turning-02.explanation: CVC § 21453(b) expressly extends the red-light turn allowance to left turns as well, when both the street you are on and the street you are entering are one-way, unless a sign forbids it. Germany has no equivalent concept: turning left on red is never permitted there, one-way streets or not. This is one of the rules German drivers find most surprising about California.

ca-turning-03.question: At a California intersection, the red light is flashing rapidly rather than staying steady. How must you behave before proceeding, for example to turn?

options.a: A flashing red means the same as a signal outage: just drive through carefully without stopping.
options.b: You must come to a complete stop, as at a stop sign, and may proceed only when it is safe and clear.
options.c: A flashing red is only a warning like flashing yellow and allows you to proceed without stopping if you are careful.
options.d: A flashing red means the signal is switched off for the night and no priority rule applies.

ca-turning-03.explanation: CVC § 21457 requires a full stop at the limit line or before the intersection when the red is flashing, after which the rules of a stop sign apply. This differs from flashing yellow, which only calls for caution without requiring a stop. In Germany, a comparable flashing red light is mainly known from railway crossings as an absolute stop-and-do-not-proceed signal, not as a regular phase at road intersections.

ca-turning-04.question: The yellow light at a California intersection is flashing rapidly instead of cycling normally from green to yellow to red. What does this mean under the California Vehicle Code?

options.a: Flashing yellow requires a full stop, as at a stop sign.
options.b: Flashing yellow applies only to left-turning drivers and bars everyone else from proceeding.
options.c: Flashing yellow means the signal is about to turn red and drivers should speed up.
options.d: Flashing yellow allows drivers to proceed through the intersection or past the signal, but only with caution.

ca-turning-04.explanation: CVC § 21457 clarifies that flashing yellow only calls for caution: proceeding is allowed without a mandatory stop, as long as the driver is careful. This resembles how a flashing yellow is treated in Germany during a signal malfunction, but in California it is a regular, intentional signal phase rather than a fault condition.

ca-turning-05.question: You are stopped at a California signal showing a steady circular green and want to make a U-turn. What applies under the California Vehicle Code?

options.a: A circular green permits proceeding straight, turning right or left, or making a U-turn, unless a sign specifically prohibits the U-turn.
options.b: U-turns on green are generally prohibited and always require a dedicated U-turn sign permitting them.
options.c: U-turns are only allowed on a red arrow, never on green.
options.d: A green light only permits going straight; any turn or U-turn requires its own green arrow.

ca-turning-05.explanation: CVC § 21451(a) explicitly lists making a U-turn among the movements permitted on a steady circular green, unless a sign prohibits it. In Germany, U-turns at intersections are also generally allowed when it can be done safely, but German traffic law addresses this mainly through general duty-of-care rules rather than naming it explicitly within the signal-light statute itself.

ca-turning-06.question: You want to make a U-turn at a signal-controlled intersection in California, where U-turns are generally permitted. Under the California Vehicle Code, from which lane must you begin the turn?

options.a: From any lane marked for your direction of travel.
options.b: Only from the far left-hand lane available for your direction of travel.
options.c: Only from the far right-hand lane, next to the curb.
options.d: From the right-turn lane, since a U-turn counts as a form of right turn.

ca-turning-06.explanation: CVC § 22100.5 requires that a U-turn at a signal-controlled intersection be made only from the far left-hand lane available for that direction of travel. German law has no comparable fixed lane requirement for U-turns; the main test there is that the maneuver happens without obstructing or endangering others.

ca-turning-07.question: At a California intersection, an official traffic control device or pavement marking indicates that a particular lane may only be used to turn left. Under the California Vehicle Code, what applies to drivers using that lane?

options.a: The marking is only a recommendation; drivers may still go straight.
options.b: Such lane requirements apply only to trucks, not to passenger cars.
options.c: It is unlawful to disobey the directions of the official traffic control device, so a driver in that lane must turn as indicated.
options.d: The requirement applies only during rush hour; outside those times drivers may choose freely.

ca-turning-07.explanation: CVC § 22101(d) makes it expressly unlawful to disobey the directions of an official traffic control device establishing mandatory turn lanes at an intersection. Germany has a comparable rule for mandatory directional lanes marked with arrows under the StVO, which are equally binding — so the underlying principle is actually similar, only the statutory source differs.

ca-turning-08.question: You are in the business district of a California city and want to make a U-turn. Under the California Vehicle Code, where is this generally allowed?

options.a: Only at an intersection, or at an opening provided in a divided roadway's median — not in the middle of the block.
options.b: Anywhere, as long as no vehicle is immediately following you.
options.c: Only in store parking lots, never on the roadway itself.
options.d: Nowhere — U-turns are completely banned in business districts in California.

ca-turning-08.explanation: CVC § 22102 restricts U-turns in business districts to intersections or to an opening specifically provided in a divided roadway's median. German law has no comparably explicit blanket restriction to intersections for busy downtown streets; there, the general duty not to endanger or obstruct other traffic governs instead.

ca-turning-09.question: You are driving in a residence district in California and want to make a U-turn mid-block, away from any signal or intersection. Another vehicle is approaching from one direction. Within what distance does the California Vehicle Code prohibit the U-turn in this situation?

options.a: Within 500 feet (about 150 meters).
options.b: Within 200 feet (about 60 meters).
options.c: Within 50 feet (about 15 meters).
options.d: There is no fixed distance, only a general duty of care as in Germany.

ca-turning-09.explanation: CVC § 22103 prohibits a U-turn in a residence district when another vehicle is approaching from either direction within 200 feet, except at an intersection with an official traffic control device. 200 feet is roughly 61 meters. German traffic law sets no fixed distance for U-turns, requiring instead only that no one be endangered or substantially obstructed — so the California rule is notably more concrete.

ca-turning-10.question: Under the California Vehicle Code, for how long before actually turning must a driver have signaled continuously?

options.a: For at least 30 seconds, regardless of distance traveled.
options.b: Only at the moment of turning; no advance warning period is required.
options.c: For at least 500 feet (about 150 meters) before the turn.
options.d: Continuously during the last 100 feet (about 30 meters) traveled by the vehicle before turning.

ca-turning-10.explanation: CVC § 22108 requires that the intention to turn be signaled continuously during the last 100 feet (about 30 meters) traveled before turning. German traffic law likewise requires signaling turns in good time and clearly, but it does not specify a fixed distance, using the general term "rechtzeitig" (in good time) instead — California turns this into a concrete distance requirement.

ca-vulnerable-01.question: A pedestrian crosses the roadway at a regular intersection where no crosswalk lines are painted (an unmarked crosswalk). What is the rule in California?

options.a: The pedestrian has no right-of-way because no crosswalk is painted.
options.b: Only children and elderly pedestrians get priority there.
options.c: The intersection is legally treated as a crosswalk, and drivers must yield to the pedestrian.
options.d: Right-of-way only exists if a pedestrian signal is installed.

ca-vulnerable-01.explanation: CVC § 21950(a) requires drivers to yield to a pedestrian crossing 'within any marked crosswalk or within any unmarked crosswalk at an intersection.' So every intersection legally counts as a crosswalk even without painted lines. Germany has no such rule: without a painted Zebrastreifen (sign 293), pedestrians at an ordinary intersection have no automatic right-of-way over traffic under StVO § 25.

ca-vulnerable-02.question: A vehicle has stopped at a crosswalk to let a pedestrian cross. What must the driver of a vehicle approaching from behind do?

options.a: Carefully overtake if the lane ahead looks clear.
options.b: Not overtake the stopped vehicle.
options.c: Overtake as long as they sound the horn first.
options.d: Overtake if no pedestrian is currently visible.

ca-vulnerable-02.explanation: CVC § 21951 flatly bars overtaking a vehicle stopped at a marked or unmarked crosswalk to let a pedestrian cross, regardless of whether the pedestrian is visible from behind — the stopped driver may see someone the overtaking driver cannot. German StVO similarly discourages overtaking near crosswalks in unclear situations, but California's rule is an unconditional ban with no visibility exception.

ca-vulnerable-03.question: A pedestrian crosses mid-block, far from any intersection or marked crosswalk ('jaywalking'). Under the CVC, who has the right-of-way?

options.a: The oncoming vehicles — the pedestrian must yield to them.
options.b: The pedestrian, as long as they looked before stepping out.
options.c: Neither — both must stop at the same time.
options.d: The pedestrian, because pedestrians always have priority in California.

ca-vulnerable-03.explanation: Outside a crosswalk, CVC § 21954(a) flips the priority: the pedestrian must yield to any vehicle close enough to be an immediate hazard. This matches the practical result under German StVO § 25(3), which requires pedestrians to cross promptly and with regard to traffic — California just gives this situation its own well-known name, jaywalking, directly in the statute.

ca-vulnerable-04.question: What is the minimum sideways clearance a car must leave when passing a cyclist traveling in the same direction in California?

options.a: 1 meter (about 3 feet), but only inside city limits.
options.b: There is no fixed distance, only a general 'safe' clearance requirement.
options.c: 1.5 meters in town and 2 meters outside town, as is customary in Germany.
options.d: At least three feet (about 0.9 m), regardless of road type.

ca-vulnerable-04.explanation: CVC § 21760, the 'Three Feet for Safety Act,' sets a concrete number in subdivision (c): at least three feet between any part of the car and any part of the bicycle or its rider. German law has no such fixed distance written into the statute; the often-quoted 1.5 m in town / 2 m outside town figures come from court rulings (Oberlandesgericht case law), not from the StVO text itself.

ca-vulnerable-05.question: A driver on a multi-lane road wants to pass a cyclist riding in their lane, and another lane going the same direction is open. What does CVC § 21760 require?

options.a: The driver may stay in the lane as long as they slow down.
options.b: The driver must change into the open lane before passing, if practicable and safe.
options.c: Changing lanes is prohibited because bicycles are not entitled to a lane of their own.
options.d: The driver must stay behind the cyclist until the cyclist leaves the roadway.

ca-vulnerable-05.explanation: CVC § 21760(c) explicitly requires changing into another available lane, 'if practicable and not prohibited by law,' before passing — not merely leaving side clearance within the same lane. German law only requires adequate lateral clearance when passing cyclists (StVO § 5(4)); it does not mandate a full lane change on multi-lane roads.

ca-vulnerable-06.question: A school bus stops on a two-lane road (no physical median) with its flashing red lights on to let children off. A car is approaching from the opposite direction. What must that driver do?

options.a: Pass carefully at reduced speed.
options.b: Stop only if following the bus, not if approaching from the opposite direction.
options.c: Also come to a stop, until the flashing red lights turn off.
options.d: Honk and continue, since the bus is stopped at the curb.

ca-vulnerable-06.explanation: CVC § 22454(a) requires drivers 'upon meeting or overtaking, from either direction' — meaning oncoming traffic too — to stop for a school bus showing its flashing red light, and to stay stopped until it turns off. Germany has no equivalent duty for oncoming traffic: a German school bus using its hazard lights (StVO § 20) only requires passing vehicles to proceed with special caution at walking speed, not to come to a full stop from the opposite direction.

ca-vulnerable-07.question: A school bus stops with its flashing red lights on, on the opposite roadway of a divided highway with a physical median. Does a driver on your own roadway also have to stop?

options.a: No — on a physically divided highway, only traffic on the bus's own roadway must stop.
options.b: Yes, always, regardless of any median.
options.c: Only if the speed limit is above 40 mph.
options.d: Yes, but only if the highway has fewer than two lanes per direction.

ca-vulnerable-07.explanation: CVC § 22454(b) carves out a clear exception: on a divided highway, or a multi-lane highway with two or more lanes per direction, a driver need not stop when the bus is on the other roadway. This refines the strict base rule in § 22454(a) and shows how finely California's rule distinguishes road types — a level of detail the German rule doesn't need, since it never imposes a full stop obligation in the first place.

ca-vulnerable-08.question: A school bus approaches a railroad crossing where no warning signal is flashing and no train is audible or visible. What does CVC § 22452 require?

options.a: The bus may proceed normally, like any other vehicle.
options.b: The bus must still stop 15 to 50 feet from the nearest rail, look both ways, and must not shift gears manually while crossing.
options.c: The bus must stop only after dark.
options.d: The bus must sound its horn but need not stop.

ca-vulnerable-08.explanation: CVC § 22452(b) requires school buses (along with certain other vehicle types, like hazmat carriers) to always stop between 15 and 50 feet from the nearest rail at every railroad crossing, whether or not any signal is active. This goes well beyond the general rule in § 22451, which only applies when a warning signal is active or a train is visible. German law has no comparable blanket stop requirement specifically for school buses at every rail crossing.

ca-vulnerable-09.question: At a railroad crossing, the crossing gates are in the process of closing. What does CVC § 22451 prohibit?

options.a: Only reversing at the crossing.
options.b: Only stopping directly on the tracks.
options.c: Nothing in particular, as long as no train is visible.
options.d: Driving through, around, or under the closed crossing gate.

ca-vulnerable-09.explanation: CVC § 22451(b) expressly bans driving 'through, around, or under any railroad or rail transit crossing gate' while it is closed, regardless of whether a train is currently visible. Subdivision (a) additionally requires stopping at least 15 feet from the nearest rail whenever a warning signal is active or a train is visible or audible and an immediate hazard. German StVO § 19 imposes a comparable ban on crossing while gates are closed or closing.

ca-vulnerable-10.question: A patrol car is parked on the shoulder with its emergency lights on (no incident blocking the roadway itself). What does CVC § 21809 require of a driver approaching in the adjacent lane?

options.a: Nothing special, as long as the vehicle isn't sitting in a travel lane.
options.b: Move over into a lane not immediately adjacent if possible, otherwise slow to a safe speed.
options.c: Come to a complete stop immediately in their own lane.
options.d: Just flash their headlights and continue at normal speed.

ca-vulnerable-10.explanation: CVC § 21809(a), California's 'Move Over' law, requires a driver passing a stationary emergency vehicle displaying emergency lights (also tow trucks or highway maintenance vehicles with flashing amber lights) to change into a lane not immediately adjacent if practicable, or, if that isn't safe, to slow to a reasonable speed. This is a different concept from Germany's 'Rettungsgasse' (StVO § 11(2)), which is about opening a lane in a traffic jam for an approaching emergency vehicle, not about passing a vehicle already stopped at the roadside.
